historic/u3e11/aaron-burr-vanderlyn.jpg.description: Aaron Burr, Jefferson's running mate who tied him 73-73 under the old two-vote electoral rules, by John Vanderlyn.

historic/u3e11/albert-gallatin.jpg.description: Albert Gallatin, Jefferson's Treasury secretary, who cut taxes including the whiskey excise Washington once marched an army to collect.

historic/u3e11/burr-hamilton-duel.jpg.description: The Burr-Hamilton duel: the 73-73 tie's aftermath, four years later.

historic/u3e11/capitol-1800.jpg.description: The U.S. Capitol in 1800: the new republic's seat, still unfinished.

historic/u3e11/hamilton-trumbull-gap2.jp.description: Alexander Hamilton by John Trumbull: the letters for Jefferson that broke the 1800 tie.

historic/u3e11/jefferson-peale-1800.jpg.description: Thomas Jefferson by Rembrandt Peale, 1800: the winner of the 36th House ballot.

historic/u3e11/john-adams-a18236.jpg.description: John Adams, who left the capital before dawn rather than attend Jefferson's inauguration.

historic/u3e11/john-marshall-met.jpg.description: Chief Justice John Marshall, who built judicial review by ruling against his own Federalist in Marbury v. Madison.

historic/u3e11/louisiana-purchase.jpg.description: Map of the Louisiana Purchase of 1803: fifteen million dollars at about three cents an acre, doubling the country overnight.

historic/u3e11/louisiana-purchase2.jpg.description: Map of the Louisiana Purchase: the fifteen-million-dollar doubling of the country.

historic/u3e11/marbury-page1.jpg.description: Page one of the Marbury v. Madison decision, 1803: the Judiciary Act provision void, judicial review claimed.

historic/u3e11/napoleon-gerard.jpg.description: Napoleon as First Consul, who sold Louisiana for fifteen million dollars after his Haitian project collapsed, by François Gérard.

historic/u3e11/toussaint-louverture.jpg.description: Toussaint Louverture, the Haitian general whose victory over Napoleon's army made Louisiana indefensible for France.

historic/u3e11/trumbull-bep.jpg.description: The Bureau of Engraving's version of Trumbull's Declaration — the painting on the back of the two-dollar bill.

historic/u3e11/twelfth-amendment.jpg.description: The Twelfth Amendment of 1804: separate ballots for president and vice president, so the 1800 tie could never happen again.
